title: White smoke from exhaust
h1: Why is white smoke coming from my exhaust?
metaDesc: White smoke from the tailpipe? Answer a few quick questions to tell normal condensation from burning coolant, see how urgent it is, and what to tell your mechanic.
intro: Thin white vapor on a cold morning is usually just water and goes away as the engine warms up. Thick white smoke that keeps coming once the engine is warm is different. It often means coolant is getting into the engine, which can lead to serious damage. These questions help you tell which one you're seeing.
safety: If the temperature gauge is in the red or a temperature warning comes on, pull over and turn off the engine.
If thick white smoke pours out and won't stop, don't keep driving. It can mean coolant is flooding into the engine.
Never open the radiator or coolant cap while the engine is hot. The coolant can spray out and burn you.

q_smoke.q: Which best describes the white smoke?
q_smoke.help: Water vapor is thin and wispy and disappears within a foot or two of the tailpipe. Smoke from burning coolant is thicker, hangs in the air, and often smells sweet.

opts.a: Thick white smoke, and the temperature gauge is high or a warning light is on
Thin, wispy vapor on a cold start that's gone once the engine warms up
Thick white smoke that keeps going even after the engine is warm
Whitish-gray smoke with a burnt oil smell
It's a diesel, and the smoke is heavy on cold starts

q_coolant.q: With the engine cold, check the coolant reservoir. Is the coolant level dropping, or does the smoke smell sweet?
q_coolant.help: The coolant reservoir is the see-through plastic tank under the hood with MIN and MAX marks. Only check it when the engine has been off for a few hours.

opts.a: Yes, I keep having to add coolant, or the smoke smells sweet
No, the coolant level stays where it should and there's no sweet smell
I haven't checked yet / I'm not sure

result.title: This sounds like normal water vapor
result.now: Watch the exhaust after the engine has fully warmed up. If the vapor is gone by then, it's usually just condensation. Keep an eye on the coolant level for the next few weeks to be sure.
if: If the white smoke is still there after a 15–20 minute drive, or gets thicker, check the coolant level when the engine is cold.
If you're adding coolant regularly, have the cooling system checked soon even if the smoke looks light.
If the temperature gauge rises above normal or a temperature warning comes on, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the smoke smells sweet, or the check engine light flashes, have it checked before driving further.
result.why: Burning fuel makes water. On cold or damp days, that water condenses in a cold exhaust and comes out as white vapor until the system heats up. It's most noticeable on short trips and in winter.

causes.name: Normal condensation in the exhaust
causes.clues: Cold or humid weather, thin vapor that fades within a few minutes, and sometimes a few drops of water from the tailpipe.
causes.against: If it stays thick after the engine is warm, condensation is less likely.

causes.name: Small coolant leak into the engine (early stage)
causes.clues: The coolant level is slowly dropping with no visible leak.
causes.against: Less likely if the coolant level stays steady for weeks.

you: Look at the exhaust after a longer drive, once fully warm.
Check the coolant reservoir level with the engine cold, and note it so you can compare in a week.
shop: Cooling system pressure test if coolant is dropping

result.title: The engine may be overheating and burning coolant
result.now: Pull over as soon as it's safe and turn off the engine. Don't drive it any further. Have it towed to a shop.
if: Keep the hood closed while steam or spray is escaping. If you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911 from there. Leave the hood closed and stay away.
If the engine cools down and the gauge looks normal, it still needs to be checked before you drive it. Restarting can make the damage worse.
result.why: Thick white smoke together with a high temperature reading often means coolant is leaking into the engine and the engine is losing its ability to cool itself. Driving an overheating engine can warp or crack major parts very quickly. A shop will usually pressure-test the cooling system and test for combustion gases before deciding on a repair.

causes.name: Blown head gasket
causes.clues: Sweet-smelling smoke, coolant that keeps disappearing, bubbles in the coolant tank.

causes.name: Cracked cylinder head or engine block
causes.clues: Overheating happened before, or the problem came on suddenly after overheating.
causes.against: Less common than a head gasket.

causes.name: Coolant leak causing the overheat
causes.clues: Coolant on the ground or steam from under the hood.

shop: Combustion gas (block) test on the coolant

result.title: Coolant may be leaking into the engine and being burned
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed to a shop and ask for a cooling system pressure test and a combustion gas test.
if: If you're stranded somewhere unsafe, call roadside assistance rather than driving on it.
If the oil on the dipstick looks milky or like chocolate milk, coolant may be mixing with the oil. Don't start the engine again.
If the temperature gauge rose while you were driving, tell the shop. They may want to check for overheating damage.
result.why: Steady white smoke with a sweet smell and a dropping coolant level often means coolant is getting into the cylinders. Each drive loses more coolant, which can lead to overheating, and coolant in the oil can quickly ruin the engine's bearings.

causes.name: Blown head gasket
causes.clues: Sweet smell, coolant loss, bubbles in the coolant tank, or rough running on startup.

causes.name: Cracked cylinder head
causes.clues: The engine has overheated in the past.

causes.name: Leaking intake manifold gasket or EGR cooler
causes.clues: Common on certain engines, and more likely on diesels for the EGR cooler.

you: With the engine off and cold, pull the oil dipstick and check for a milky, light-brown color.
Note how much coolant you've had to add and how often.

result.title: Could be heavy condensation, but worth a check if it continues
result.now: Keep an eye on the coolant level each week and book a check if the smoke doesn't clear up after longer drives.
if: If the coolant level starts dropping or the smoke starts smelling sweet, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the check engine light flashes or the engine runs rough, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: With no coolant loss and no sweet smell, a serious coolant leak is less likely. Lots of short trips in cold or humid weather can keep the exhaust from ever fully drying out, so vapor lasts longer than you'd expect.

causes.name: Heavy condensation from short trips
causes.clues: Mostly short drives, cold or humid weather, water dripping from the tailpipe.

causes.name: Small oil burning (whitish-gray smoke)
causes.clues: A burnt oil smell, or the oil level dropping between changes.

causes.name: Very slow internal coolant leak
causes.clues: The level drops a little over several weeks.
causes.against: Less likely if the level is truly steady.

you: Mark the coolant level and check it weekly with the engine cold.
Check the oil dipstick for a low level or milky color.
shop: Exhaust smoke check on a warm engine

result.title: Check the coolant and oil before driving it again
result.now: Avoid driving it until you've checked. Once the engine is completely cool, check the coolant reservoir and the oil dipstick. If the coolant is low, the oil looks milky, or you can't check, have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to look at it.
if: If the coolant is low or the oil looks milky, don't start it again. Have it towed.
If the temperature gauge rises above normal at any point, pull over and turn off the engine.
Even with a normal coolant level and normal-looking oil, continued white smoke needs inspection before another drive.
result.why: Thick white smoke after warm-up is often coolant being burned, and the coolant level is the quickest clue. Until you know, it's safest not to drive it, so a coolant leak doesn't turn into an overheated engine.

causes.name: Coolant leaking into the engine
causes.clues: A sweet smell, dropping coolant, or a temperature gauge that creeps up.

causes.name: Heavy condensation
causes.clues: Cold weather and short trips, with smoke that thins out on longer drives.

causes.name: Oil burning
causes.clues: Grayish smoke with a burnt oil smell.

you: Check the coolant level through the marked reservoir only when the engine is fully cold.
With the engine off and cold, note whether the oil looks milky.

result.title: Grayish smoke with a burnt oil smell often means oil is being burned
result.now: Check the oil level on the dipstick and top it up if it's low. Have the engine checked within a few days.
if: If the oil warning light comes on or the engine starts knocking, pull over and turn off the engine. Don't restart it.
If the smoke is coming from under the hood rather than the tailpipe, pull over, turn the engine off and step away. Oil on the hot exhaust can catch fire. Have it inspected before driving again.
If the oil level was very low, or the check engine light is flashing, have it checked before driving further.
result.why: Burning oil often looks blue-gray, but in some light it looks whitish. The burnt oil smell is a strong clue. Oil can get into the cylinders past worn seals or rings, or through a turbocharger or a faulty PCV valve.

causes.name: Worn valve stem seals or piston rings
causes.clues: You add oil between changes, and there's a puff of smoke on startup or when accelerating.

causes.name: Faulty PCV valve
causes.clues: Oil in the air intake, or a whistling or rough idle.

causes.name: Leaking turbocharger seals (turbo engines)
causes.clues: Smoke when accelerating hard, and oil in the intake pipes.

you: Check the oil level with the engine off on level ground.
Note whether the smoke shows up on startup, when accelerating, or all the time.

result.title: On a diesel, cold-start white smoke is often unburned fuel
result.now: Wait for the glow plug light to go out before starting, and book a check if the smoke is heavy or lasts more than a few minutes.
if: If the smoke continues once fully warm, or the coolant level drops, have it checked within a few days.
If the engine is hard to start, runs rough, or the check engine light is on, get it checked soon.
If the smoke smells sweet or the temperature gauge rises, pull over and turn off the engine.
result.why: A diesel relies on heat from compression to ignite its fuel. When the engine is cold, some fuel may not burn fully and comes out as white smoke. Weak glow plugs or worn injectors make this worse.

causes.name: Weak or failed glow plugs
causes.clues: Hard starts in cold weather, rough running for the first minute, and smoke that clears as it warms.

causes.name: Worn or leaking fuel injectors
causes.clues: Rough idle, a raw diesel smell, or poor fuel economy.

causes.name: Coolant leaking into the cylinders
causes.clues: Sweet smell, coolant loss, and smoke that continues when warm.
causes.against: Less likely if the coolant level is steady.

you: Note whether the glow plug light stays on longer than usual or flashes.
Check the coolant level with the engine cold.
shop: Glow plug and glow plug relay test
Cooling system pressure test if coolant is dropping
